```{r}
#| include: false
library(tidyverse)
library(knitr)
library(here)
```

## What is being compared

`final_data.csv` was built in the week 3 in-class assignment by
`R/create_final_data.R`, which uses the tidyverse: `pivot_longer()` for the
World Bank files, `pivot_wider()` for the disaster indicators, `group_by()` and
`summarise()` for the conflict deaths, and `left_join()` to merge.

`final_data_agent.csv` was built by `R/create_final_data_agent.R`, which a
coding agent wrote from the same written specification without reusing any of
that code. It uses base R only: `reshape()`, `aggregate()`, `merge()` and
`split()`. The point of writing it twice in two different dialects is that an
error in one implementation is unlikely to repeat itself in the other, so any
disagreement between the two outputs points at something worth checking.

```{r}
own <- read.csv(here("data", "processed", "final_data.csv"))
agent <- read.csv(here("data", "processed", "final_data_agent.csv"))
```

## Shape and column names

```{r}
tibble(
  Check = c("Rows", "Columns", "Column names identical", "Column order identical"),
  Own = c(nrow(own), ncol(own), "", ""),
  Agent = c(nrow(agent), ncol(agent), "", ""),
  Agree = c(nrow(own) == nrow(agent),
            ncol(own) == ncol(agent),
            setequal(names(own), names(agent)),
            identical(names(own), names(agent)))
) |>
  kable(caption = "Dimensions and column names")
```

Both files have 3720 rows, which is exactly 186 countries times 20 years
(2000 to 2019). That is the balanced panel the paper describes, so neither
build dropped or duplicated a country-year.

## Cell by cell comparison

```{r}
agent <- agent[, names(own)]
own <- own[order(own$iso, own$year), ]
agent <- agent[order(agent$iso, agent$year), ]
row.names(own) <- NULL
row.names(agent) <- NULL

comparison <- all.equal(own, agent)
identical_output <- isTRUE(comparison)
identical_output
```

```{r}
mismatch_count <- function(x, y) {
  both_na <- is.na(x) & is.na(y)
  sum(!both_na & (is.na(x) != is.na(y) | x != y), na.rm = TRUE)
}

map_int(names(own), \(v) mismatch_count(own[[v]], agent[[v]])) |>
  set_names(names(own)) |>
  enframe(name = "Variable", value = "Disagreeing cells") |>
  kable(caption = "Number of country-years where the two builds disagree")
```

Every column agrees in every one of the 3720 rows, missing values included.
The two implementations produce the same data set.

## Checks on the derived variables

Agreement between two implementations only shows that they made the same
choices. The checks below ask whether those choices match the paper.

```{r}
tibble(
  Quantity = c("Countries", "Years", "Country-years with armed conflict",
               "Country-years with an earthquake",
               "Country-years with a drought",
               "First year of lagged exposure that is missing"),
  Value = c(n_distinct(own$iso),
            paste(min(own$year), "to", max(own$year)),
            sum(own$armedconflict),
            sum(own$earthquake),
            sum(own$drought),
            sum(is.na(own$armedconflict_lag1)))
) |>
  kable(caption = "Derived quantities in the merged data")
```

The lagged exposure is missing for exactly 186 rows, one per country, which is
the year 2000 row where no earlier year exists. The lag was computed within
country, so no country inherits the previous country's last value.

```{r}
own |>
  filter(iso %in% c("AFG", "CAN")) |>
  group_by(iso) |>
  slice_head(n = 3) |>
  select(iso, year, armedconflict, armedconflict_lag1) |>
  kable(caption = "The lag resets at each country")
```

## Where the two builds could have diverged

Three judgment calls in the specification are not fully determined by the
assignment text. Both builds resolved them the same way, so they do not show up
as disagreements between the two files, but each of them changes the data if
resolved differently, and they are the first places to look if these numbers do
not match a classmate's.

### Which year column defines a disaster

```{r}
dis_raw <- read.csv(here("data", "raw", "disaster.csv"), check.names = TRUE) |>
  filter(Disaster.Type %in% c("Earthquake", "Drought"))

tibble(
  Check = c("Earthquake and drought rows in the file",
            "Rows kept by `Year` in 2000 to 2019",
            "Rows kept by `Start Year` in 2000 to 2019",
            "Rows where `Year` and `Start Year` differ"),
  Rows = c(nrow(dis_raw),
           sum(dis_raw$Year >= 2000 & dis_raw$Year <= 2019),
           sum(dis_raw$Start.Year >= 2000 & dis_raw$Start.Year <= 2019),
           sum(dis_raw$Year != dis_raw$Start.Year, na.rm = TRUE))
) |>
  kable(caption = "Disaster year: the `Year` column versus the `Start Year` column")
```

The two columns are not interchangeable. They disagree on 25 rows, all of them
droughts, where EM-DAT records the year the drought was entered under and a
later year as the year it began.

```{r}
dis_raw |>
  filter(Year != Start.Year) |>
  count(Disaster.Type, name = "Rows") |>
  kable(caption = "Which disaster types have a `Year` that differs from `Start Year`")
```

The table below rebuilds the disaster indicators under each choice.

```{r}
build_disaster <- function(year_col) {
  keep <- dis_raw[dis_raw[[year_col]] >= 2000 & dis_raw[[year_col]] <= 2019, ]
  data.frame(iso = keep$ISO,
             year = keep[[year_col]],
             type = keep$Disaster.Type) |>
    distinct() |>
    mutate(value = 1) |>
    pivot_wider(names_from = type, values_from = value, values_fill = 0) |>
    janitor::clean_names()
}

by_year <- build_disaster("Year")
by_start <- build_disaster("Start.Year")

differing <- full_join(by_year, by_start, by = c("iso", "year"),
                       suffix = c("_year", "_start")) |>
  mutate(across(where(is.numeric), \(x) replace_na(x, 0))) |>
  filter(earthquake_year != earthquake_start | drought_year != drought_start)

tibble(
  Quantity = c("Country-years with a disaster",
               "Earthquake country-years",
               "Drought country-years"),
  `Using Year` = c(nrow(by_year), sum(by_year$earthquake), sum(by_year$drought)),
  `Using Start Year` = c(nrow(by_start), sum(by_start$earthquake),
                         sum(by_start$drought))
) |>
  kable(caption = "The disaster indicators under each year definition")
```

```{r}
nrow(differing)
```

Switching to `Start Year` would move `r nrow(differing)` country-years, all of
them droughts. Both builds use `Year`, which is what the week 3 instructions
named, so the two files agree, but this is a real choice with a real effect and
not a difference that can be ignored.

### Repeated disasters within one country-year

```{r}
dis_raw |>
  filter(Year >= 2000, Year <= 2019) |>
  count(ISO, Year, Disaster.Type) |>
  summarise(`Country-year-type combinations` = n(),
            `Of those, with more than one event` = sum(n > 1),
            `Largest number of events in one country-year` = max(n)) |>
  pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = "Check", values_to = "Count") |>
  kable(caption = "Repeated disasters in the same country and year")
```

Both builds collapse these to a single indicator rather than a count, so a
country-year with three earthquakes is coded 1. The week 3 version does this
with `distinct()` before `pivot_wider()`, the agent version with `max()` inside
`aggregate()`, and the two give the same answer.

### The conflict threshold

```{r}
conflict_raw <- read.csv(here("data", "raw", "conflict.csv"))

conflict_cy <- conflict_raw |>
  group_by(iso, year) |>
  summarise(deaths = sum(best, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop")

conflict_cy |>
  summarise(`Country-years in the conflict file` = n(),
            `Reaching 25 deaths` = sum(deaths >= 25),
            `Below 25 deaths` = sum(deaths < 25)) |>
  pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = "Check", values_to = "Count") |>
  kable(caption = "The conflict file collapsed to country-years")
```

Both builds sum `best` over every conflict active in a country-year and code
the exposure as 1 when the total reaches 25 battle related deaths, which is the
UCDP definition the paper uses. Summing before thresholding matters: a country
with three separate conflicts of ten deaths each is exposed under this rule and
would not be if each conflict were tested on its own.

## One number that does not reconcile with the paper

The paper reports 522 country-years of minor conflict and 148 of war, which is
670 exposed country-years. This data set has 665.

```{r}
exposed <- conflict_cy |> filter(deaths >= 25)

tibble(
  Source = c("Paper (522 minor + 148 war)",
             "Conflict file, 25 death threshold, all years",
             "Conflict file, 25 death threshold, 2000 to 2019",
             "In final_data.csv after the merge"),
  `Country-years` = c(670,
                      nrow(exposed),
                      sum(exposed$year >= 2000 & exposed$year <= 2019),
                      sum(own$armedconflict))
) |>
  kable(caption = "Reconciling the exposure count against the paper")
```

```{r}
exposed |>
  filter(year >= 2000, year <= 2019) |>
  anti_join(own, by = c("iso", "year")) |>
  nrow()
```

The merge loses nothing: every exposed country-year in 2000 to 2019 survives
into `final_data.csv`, and the drop from 704 to 665 is entirely years outside
the study window. So the five country-year gap against the paper is not a
merge problem and not something either implementation introduced.

The disaster indicators do lose a few country-years at the merge, because some
ISO codes in EM-DAT have no World Bank mortality data.

```{r}
tibble(
  Indicator = c("Earthquake", "Drought"),
  `Before the merge` = c(sum(by_year$earthquake), sum(by_year$drought)),
  `In final_data.csv` = c(sum(own$earthquake), sum(own$drought))
) |>
  kable(caption = "Disaster country-years lost to countries with no mortality data")
```

Those countries have no outcome to contribute and cannot enter the analysis, so
dropping them is correct rather than a loss.

## Conclusion

Two independent implementations, one in the tidyverse and one in base R,
produce identical output: 3720 rows, 18 columns, no disagreeing cells. The
derived variables behave as intended, the lag resets at each country, and the
indicator zeros are true zeros rather than unknowns. No edit to
`final_data.csv` is needed.

Two things are worth raising in class. The first is that `Year` and `Start Year`
in the EM-DAT file disagree on 25 drought rows, and choosing one over the other
moves 21 country-years of the drought indicator. The second is the five
country-year gap between this data set's 665 exposed country-years and the
paper's 670; the merge accounts for none of it, so it is most likely a
difference in the vintage of the UCDP release or in how the countries the paper
excludes were handled, and the code cannot settle it.
